I want to directly quote their page at Star Trek Fan Films and clearly make my own concerns known prior to offering a few solutions. Going with the quote here!

CBS and Paramount Pictures are big believers in reasonable fan fiction and fan creativity, and, in particular, want amateur fan filmmakers to showcase their passion for Star Trek. Therefore CBS and Paramount Pictures will not object to, or take legal action against, Star Trek fan productions that are non-professional and amateur and meet the following guidelines.

I have to say, now that we’re into this that I’m going to take all of this with a little grain of bullshit for a few reasons. First, these guidelines were created in direct response to the Axanar film. I’ll show you exactly where they’re outright lying and promoting an agenda at the same time.

Guidelines for Avoiding Objections 1. The fan production must be less than 15 minutes for a single self-contained story, or no more than 2 segments, episodes or parts, not to exceed 30 minutes total, with no additional seasons, episodes, parts, sequels or remakes.

Here we have an arbitrary time frame that is not only unresonable, it’s ridiculous. Considering that this particular series has been around since forever and now resides on the chopping block. Enjoy while you can…StarTrekContinues.

  1. The title of the fan production or any parts cannot include the name “Star Trek.” However, the title must contain a subtitle with the phrase: “A STAR TREK FAN PRODUCTION” in plain typeface. The fan production cannot use the term “official” in either its title or subtitle or in any marketing, promotions or social media for the fan production.

Another unreasonable “guideline” considering the series mentioned previously.

  1. The content in the fan production must be original, not reproductions, recreations or clips from any Star Trek production. If non-Star Trek third party content is used, all necessary permissions for any third party content should be obtained in writing.

This one I kind of understand and this is one that I think is reasonable and would recommend that fans making fan films follow if they’re so inclined. This one just makes sense because it does protect CBS’s property along with the property of anyone else that might find one of their characters or settings used.

  1. If the fan production uses commercially-available Star Trek uniforms, accessories, toys and props, these items must be official merchandise and not bootleg items or imitations of such commercially available products.

You can make that uniform on the cheap? Tough shit, bud, you have to buy all official merch for that fan film. They don’t want to be associated with you but they’ll damn sure take your money for it.

  1. The fan production must be a real “fan” production, i.e., creators, actors and all other participants must be amateurs, cannot be compensated for their services, and cannot be currently or previously employed on any Star Trek series, films, production of DVDs or with any of CBS or Paramount Pictures’ licensees.

Tony Todd was in the Prelude To Axanar film on YouTube. Did he get any compensation?   1. The fan production must be non-commercial:

    CBS and Paramount Pictures do not object to limited fundraising for the creation of a fan production, whether 1 or 2 segments and consistent with these guidelines, so long as the total amount does not exceed $50,000, including all platform fees, and when the $50,000 goal is reached, all fundraising must cease. The fan production must only be exhibited or distributed on a no-charge basis and/or shared via streaming services without generating revenue. The fan production cannot be distributed in a physical format such as DVD or Blu-ray. No unlicensed Star Trek-related or fan production-related merchandise or services can be offered for sale or given away as premiums, perks or rewards or in connection with the fan production fundraising. The fan production cannot derive revenue by selling or licensing fan-created production sets, props or costumes.

So you can’t make money on it. You can crowdfund but not to exceed $50k AND you have to buy all uniforms and props through official channels. Jesus Christ, does CBS want in or out? That means your only real means of getting this thing shown if it’s completed and is put together well is YouTube, discover, upload and monetize original videos or Kodi. Star Trek fans are a pretty tech savvy lot in majority but really. This means you won’t see it on Netflix, Hulu or any other mainstream streaming service. My question on this is Was Anyone Actually Trying To Get Their Films Released For Money? Also, as an added bonus. you are either stuck with or must destroy any of the props, sets and other related merch that you purchased. You cannot resell it or give it away. You cannot make your money back on the stuff you’ve paid for reducing your cost to even $0.
